title: Healthy Volunteers Faked One Symptom, Yet Hospital Wards Could Not Tell
description:
Experimental Chronicle — David Rosenhan (1973): 'On Being Sane in Insane Places', Diagnostic Stickiness & Susannah Cahalan's Archival Investigation, grounded in D. L. Rosenhan (1973) (Science). Empirical findings show that in January 1973, Stanford professor David Rosenhan published 'On Being Sane in Insane Places' in Science, reporting that eight healthy 'pseudopatients' presented at 12 psychiatric hospitals complaining ONLY of hearing a vague voice say 'empty,' 'hollow,' and 'thud'.

Follow-up physiological and behavioral evidence demonstrates: According to Rosenhan's report, the instant each pseudopatient stepped onto the ward, they stopped simulating any symptom whatsoever, acted completely calm and cooperative, and said the voices were gone.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- D. L. Rosenhan (1973). On Being Sane in Insane Places. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.179.4070.250
- Curwyn Mapaling (2024). The Night Nurse: A reflection on On Being Sane in Insane Places by D. L. Rosenhan (1973). Scholarship of Teaching and Learning in the South. https://doi.org/10.36615/sotls.v8i1.366
- Robert L. Spitzer (1975). On pseudoscience in science, logic in remission, and psychiatric diagnosis: A critique of Rosenhan's "On being sane in insane places". Journal of Abnormal Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0077124
